newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians looted long-range missiles - army source.
newsitem.headline: Albanians looted long-range missiles - army source.

text.p: Albanian thieves have stolen long-range battlefield missiles from a garrison near the border with Greece, local military sources said on Tuesday.
Defence Ministry spokesman Pandeli Ristani told national television "a quantity of special ammunition has been stolen" but gave no further details.
"A group of experts has gone to the Gjirokaster division and they will provide further information when they return," Ristani said.

Military sources from the southern Laberia Division, who chose to remain anonymous, told local reporters 15 out of 40 long-range missiles had been stolen on Sunday at dawn after thieves broke open the iron gate of an underground tunnel.
They said the surface-to-surface and surface-to-air missiles had been imported from China in 1995.
"All the Kalashnikovs that have looted are nothing compared to this," an army commander was quoted as saying.

A British defence expert, Paul Beaver of Jane's Information Group, told Reuters in London the surface-to-surface missiles were almost certainly the land-based version of the Silkworm, which has a range of around 70 km (45 miles) and has been exported by China to a number of countries.
An estimated one million weapons are in private hands after armouries were broken open in March when protests by investors in fraudulent pyramid schemes degenerated into violence.
The sources said the thieves had taken the missiles, the beds on which they rest, their ignition mechanism and their target-locating mechanism.
It was not known whether the thieves knew how to use the missiles but they had taken away an instruction manual.
A group of Albanian officers trained for six months in China to use "the most sophisticated weapons the Albanian army possesses", the source added.

Beaver said the weapons would be difficult to target: "You have to know exactly where you are on the map before you can send it off," he added. He estimated the total cost of the Albanian deal with China at $10 million.
The army division responsible for the missiles reported directly to the ex-communist country's chiefs of staff.

If confirmed, the rocket looting would be the worst in a string of incidents to affect Albania's armed forces, which put up practically no resistance when people stormed depots and took away light and heavy weapons, bombs and explosives.
A government of National Reconciliation formed in March to save the country chaos and anarchy tried to boost the army's morale by reorganising many units.
